\chapter{Tomorrow, and Good Night}
\label{ch:pa-tomorrow-and-goodnight}
\hlchaptermodality{36}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can promise to meet tomorrow with kall milaange, explain why kall also means yesterday and what settles the direction, say good night formally with shubh raat while knowing it is not the commonest parting, and write shubh raat in Gurmukhi.}

The reader gives the formal good night, states that it belongs to the formal register rather than to ordinary doorstep speech, traces raat to Sanskrit ratri, runs every parting the book has taught, and writes both words from memory after the short hook has been traced.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kall milāṁge]{kall milāṁge — one word for both sides of today}

\label{lesson:PA-C36-kall-milaange}



\begin{quote}
Part twice: \textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ} \pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ} \pa{ਜੀ}}. One names a time, one does not. This session names a time exactly — and then takes half of that back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\emph{kall} — \textbf{tomorrow; yesterday}
\end{quote}

Both. One word, one day away from today, and no direction built in.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Kall} comes down from Sanskrit \emph{kalya}, \textquotedblleft{}daybreak, the morrow.\textquotedblright{} Along the way it stopped choosing a side. A Punjabi speaker who says \emph{kall} has named the day adjacent to this one, and the listener works out which one from the verb.

Say \emph{kall milāṁge}, with \emph{milāṁge} pointing forward — we \textbf{will} meet — and \emph{kall} is tomorrow. Say it with a past verb and the same \emph{kall} is yesterday. The word supplies the distance; the verb supplies the direction.

Hindi keeps the identical arrangement, and it strikes speakers of English as strange until they notice English doing something close with \emph{next}: \emph{next Friday} can mean two different Fridays, and only the surrounding sentence decides.

So this parting has to carry its verb. \emph{Jaldī} — the borrowed word, Persian \emph{jald} under a Persian ending — could stand nearly alone and still mean soon. \emph{Kall}, inherited and older, would leave the listener a day out in either direction.

On the page \emph{kall} needs one mark this book has not taught — a small hook that tucks a letter underneath another. It stays in sound here.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kall milāṁge} — see you tomorrow
  \item \emph{State:} the second meaning of \emph{kall} (yesterday)
  \item \emph{Explain:} what tells a listener which one is meant (the verb)
  \item \emph{Run through:} four partings — \emph{phir milāṁge}, \emph{changā jī}, \emph{jaldī milāṁge}, \emph{kall milāṁge}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Promise to meet tomorrow. (\emph{Kall milāṁge}.) What else can \emph{kall} mean? (Yesterday.) What decides? (The verb.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%95\%E0\%A9\%B1\%E0\%A8\%B2\%E0\%A9\%8D\%E0\%A8\%B9}{Wiktionary: kall}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%AF}{Wiktionary: kalya}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[u]{\pa{ੁ} — the shorter of the two hooks}

\label{lesson:PA-W09-aunkar}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\pa{ਨੂ}} once, with the long hook underneath. Then write \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼}}, the \emph{sh} letter carrying its dot below.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one mark}
Take one stroke off the hook and the vowel shortens: \textbf{\pa{ੁ}}, the \textbf{auṅkaṛ}, sounds a short \emph{u}. Trace \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁ}} twice and say \emph{shu}.

Hold the two below-the-line marks side by side once and say them: \emph{shu} short, \emph{nū} long. The page counts strokes; the ear counts length.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Cover the models. Write \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁ}}, then \textbf{\pa{ਨੂ}}. Compare only how far each mark reaches below the letter.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The last of the four below-and-above pairs this chapter needed.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shubh rāt]{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ} \pa{ਰਾਤ} — an auspicious night, and where it belongs}

\label{lesson:PA-C36-shubh-raat}



\begin{quote}
Part three ways: \textbf{\pa{ਚੰਗਾ} \pa{ਜੀ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਜਲਦੀ} \pa{ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ}}, \emph{kall milāṁge}. All three can be said at any hour. One parting is left, and it can be said at only one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one phrase}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ} \pa{ਰਾਤ}} — \emph{shubh rāt} — \textbf{good night}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਸ਼}} with the short hook under it, then \textbf{\pa{ਭ}}: \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ}}. Then \textbf{\pa{ਰ}}, the upright \textbf{\pa{ਾ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਤ}}: \textbf{\pa{ਰਾਤ}}. Every shape has been traced, the last of them in the session before this one.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ}} is Sanskrit \emph{śubha}, \textquotedblleft{}auspicious, splendid, good.\textquotedblright{} It is the word that opens a wedding invitation and a festival greeting, and it carries a sense English \emph{good} does not: not merely pleasant, but well-omened.

\textbf{\pa{ਰਾਤ}} comes down from Sanskrit \emph{rātri}, \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} worn smooth on the way — the long middle collapsed, and the word ends on the \emph{t}.

Both halves are inherited, which makes this parting unusual in a book whose farewells have kept crossing traditions. The blessing farewell \emph{rabb rākhā} pairs an Arabic word for God with an inherited verb; the two words for thanks come in a Sanskritic and a Perso-Arabic version side by side. Here both pieces come down the same line.

One thing must be said plainly, because a phrasebook would leave it out. \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ} \pa{ਰਾਤ}} belongs to the formal register — writing, broadcast, a careful goodbye to someone you address respectfully. At a Punjabi door at night you are more likely to hear \emph{rabb rākhā}, or the English \emph{good night} borrowed whole. Knowing the formal phrase is worth having; mistaking it for the common one is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: assemble \pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ} \pa{ਰਾਤ}}
Look at \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ} \pa{ਰਾਤ}} for a moment, then cover it and write both words from memory. Uncover and compare two things only: whether the dot sits under the first letter, and whether the hook sits under it as well. Then write \textbf{\pa{ਮੈਨੂੰ}} once more underneath — the only other word in this run that carries marks both above and below.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shubh rāt} — good night
  \item \emph{State:} which register it belongs to, and what is said more often instead
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \textbf{\pa{ਰਾਤ}} back to its Sanskrit ancestor (\emph{rātri})
  \item \emph{Run through:} all four partings from this run, and the two learned earlier
  \item \emph{Recall:} the Sanskrit word behind \emph{kall} (\emph{kalya}, \textquotedblleft{}daybreak\textquotedblright{}) beside \emph{rātri}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say good night formally. (\textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ} \pa{ਰਾਤ}}.) What does \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਭ}} add beyond \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}? (Auspicious, well-omened.) Which Sanskrit word is \textbf{\pa{ਰਾਤ}}? (\emph{Rātri}.) Write both words once from memory.

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B6\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%AD}{Wiktionary: shubh}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%B0\%E0\%A8\%BE\%E0\%A8\%A4}{Wiktionary: raat}.
\end{tcolorbox}
